name: Council of Trent
summary: The Catholic Church's council in response to the Protestant Reformation, which defined Catholic teaching against Protestant doctrines and launched wide-ranging reforms.
place: Trento, Prince-Bishopric of Trent (modern Italy); briefly Bologna (1547–1549)

key_dates.label: Decree on justification; council moved to Bologna
Second period opens; decree on the Eucharist
Third period opens; decree on the Mass

background.text: Luther and other reformers had called for a free general council since 1518; years of conflict between the papacy, Charles V, and France delayed it.

happened.text: The council met in three periods: 1545–1547 (moved to Bologna in 1547) under Paul III, 1551–1552 under Julius III, and 1562–1563 under Pius IV; attendance was small at first, rising to over 200 bishops at the end, most of them Italian.

In April 1546 it declared Scripture and unwritten tradition both to be received with equal reverence, fixed the canon including the deuterocanonical books, and made the Latin Vulgate the authoritative text.
In January 1547 it issued its decree on justification, rejecting justification by faith alone with 33 canons pronouncing anathema on those who taught it.
It affirmed seven sacraments, transubstantiation (1551), and the Mass as a true sacrifice (1562), each with anathemas on opposing views.
Protestant delegates from Württemberg, Strasbourg, and Saxony came to the second period in 1551–1552 under safe conduct, but no real debate took place.
In 1563 it required bishops to live in their dioceses, ordered a seminary in each diocese to train priests, and regulated marriage (the decree Tametsi).

participants.name: Paul III, Julius III, Pius IV
participants.role: Popes who convened and resumed it; none attended in person

participants.name: Giovanni Morone
participants.role: Papal legate who steered the final period to a close

participants.name: Reginald Pole
participants.role: One of the first papal legates

participants.name: Charles Borromeo
participants.role: Pius IV's nephew and secretary of state; later a leading enforcer of the decrees

participants.name: Martin Luther
participants.role: Not present; died in 1546, two months after the council opened, and its decrees on justification and Scripture answered his teaching

participants.name: Martin Chemnitz
participants.role: Not present; wrote the four-volume Lutheran reply, Examination of the Council of Trent (1565–1573)

participants.name: John Calvin
participants.role: Not present; wrote a Protestant reply, Acts of the Council of Trent with the Antidote (1547)

outcomes.text: Its decrees defined Catholic teaching for four centuries, until the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965), which did not revoke them.
It led to the Roman Catechism (1566), a revised Missal (1570), and a revised Vulgate (1592), giving the Catholic Church a uniform liturgy.
It confirmed the division between Catholics and Protestants; Protestants rejected it as neither free nor general.

condemnations_note: Trent condemned doctrines, not named people. Its canons pronounce 'let him be anathema' on anyone holding the listed Protestant positions. In 1999 the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification between the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation stated that the condemnations of the 16th century on justification do not apply to the teaching of the Lutheran churches as set out in that declaration.

condemnations.authority: General council of the Catholic Church
condemnations.reason: 33 canons pronouncing anathema on teachings about justification, including justification by faith alone
condemnations.status: Remain in force; the 1999 Joint Declaration says they do not apply to the Lutheran teaching it describes

condemnations.authority: General council of the Catholic Church
condemnations.reason: Anathemas on Protestant teachings about the sacraments, the Eucharist, the Mass, and the priesthood

persecution_note: The council itself did not try or punish anyone. The Roman Inquisition and the Index of Prohibited Books, which enforced Catholic teaching in this period, were separate institutions run by the papacy.
